issue.description:
README.md:41-46 advertises a per-session spend cap (5 USD), hourly spend cap (50 USD), and a 100 USD circuit breaker that disables new sessions. None of these are actually enforced:

- activate_circuit_breaker (app/middleware/cost_protection.py:340) has ZERO callers anywhere in app/ — the breaker can never trip. The check in handle_media_stream (app/main.py:453-472) and CostProtectionMiddleware.__call__ only reacts to a flag that is never set.
- total_cost_last_hour (cost_protection.py:131) is initialized to 0.0 and never updated; max_total_cost_per_hour_usd is never compared against anything.
- check_budget (cost_protection.py:287) computes budget_ok / duration_ok, but every caller of track_usage discards the returned budget status: app/main.py:756-763 (web_search) wraps it in try/except-pass, and app/memory.py:314-321 and :470-477 do the same. A session that exceeds the 5 USD cap or the 30-minute max duration keeps running untouched.

Fix scope:
1. Accumulate hourly total cost in track_usage (rolling window or hour bucket) and call activate_circuit_breaker when circuit_breaker_threshold_usd is crossed; also enforce max_total_cost_per_hour_usd by refusing new sessions.
2. When track_usage returns budget_ok=False for a session, act on it: send an error frame and close that WebSocket session (or refuse further tool calls) instead of ignoring it.
3. Enforce max_session_duration_minutes (currently computed in check_budget but never acted on — a duration watchdog task in handle_media_stream is acceptable).
4. calculate_cost (cost_protection.py:196-208) only recognizes gpt-5 / gpt-5-mini / gpt-realtime, but the code actually passes gpt-5.4-nano (app/main.py:757, app/memory.py:316) which silently falls into the unknown-model branch with a warning per call — add the actually-used model names to the pricing table.

Acceptance criteria (run inside the repo):
1. Unit test: driving track_usage past circuit_breaker_threshold_usd sets circuit_breaker_active=True and a subsequent session is rejected.
2. Unit test: a session whose accumulated cost exceeds max_session_cost_usd gets terminated / its next tool call refused.
3. Unit test: calculate_cost returns non-default pricing for gpt-5.4-nano without logging an unknown-model warning.
4. Existing tests/test_cost_protection.py and tests/integration/test_cost_protection_integration.py pass.
issue.title: Enforce advertised cost caps: wire circuit breaker activation and act on check_budget results

issue.description:
app/main.py starts cost tracking for every /session WebSocket (await cost_tracker.start_session(session_id), app/main.py:450) but end_session is only ever called on the circuit-breaker rejection path (app/main.py:471). The normal path — await session.run() at app/main.py:1121-1136 — returns or raises without ever calling end_session.

Consequences (see app/middleware/cost_protection.py:161-179): the active_sessions Prometheus gauge is incremented in start_session (line 139) and only decremented in end_session (line 168), so the gauge grows monotonically and the metric is useless; session_costs, session_tokens, and session_start_times dicts retain an entry per session forever (unbounded memory growth in a long-lived pod); session_duration histogram never records completed sessions.

Fix: wrap the session lifetime in try/finally in handle_media_stream so that await cost_tracker.end_session(session_id) runs on normal disconnect, runtime error, and any early-return path after start_session.

Acceptance criteria (run inside the repo):
1. A new unit/integration test (e.g. in tests/test_cost_protection.py or tests/integration/) connects a WebSocket via FastAPI TestClient with a mocked OpenAI ephemeral-key call, disconnects, and asserts end_session was called (tracker dicts no longer contain the session_id).
2. A test asserts end_session is also called when session.run() raises.
3. pytest tests/test_cost_protection.py passes; full pytest suite does not regress.

issue.close_reason: Fixed: Use JWT-derived user_display_name in memory system message. Changed app/main.py:555 to use user_display_name (JWT-aware) instead of recomputing from forwarded headers, and app/main.py:558 to base email parenthetical on user_identity instead of forwarded_email. Added 3 integration tests verifying JWT identity works correctly, header-based path still works, and JWT takes priority over headers. All tests pass (16/16 in test_memory_websocket_e2e.py). issue.description:
app/main.py:429-437 correctly computes user_identity and user_display_name with JWT identity taking priority over x-forwarded-* proxy headers. But when the system message is built for a user with a memory store, app/main.py:535 recomputes the display name from proxy headers only:

    user_display = forwarded_name or forwarded_email or forwarded_user

In production (per CLAUDE.md Deployment notes) the /session route is excluded from Traefik forward-auth, so x-forwarded-user/email/name are never set there and JWT-via-query-param is the only identity path that can work. In exactly that path, all three forwarded_* values are empty strings, so user_display is empty and the injected memory section reads: 'The current user is .' — the model is told nothing about who the user is even though jwt_user_info carries email and name. The follow-up check at app/main.py:538 (if forwarded_email and forwarded_email != user_display) has the same header-only blind spot.

Fix: replace the recomputation at app/main.py:535 with the already-computed user_display_name (falling back to user_identity), and base the parenthesized-email check on the JWT/header-agnostic user_identity value.

Acceptance criteria (run inside the repo):
1. Unit/integration test: connect to /session with a valid JWT in the token query param (no x-forwarded-* headers), a memory store containing at least one fact, and assert the system_message passed to RealtimeSession contains the JWT email/name and does NOT contain the string 'The current user is .'
2. Existing header-based path still works: test with x-forwarded-email set and no JWT asserts the header-derived name appears.
3. pytest passes (tests/integration/test_memory_websocket_e2e.py must not regress).
issue.title: Use JWT-derived user_display_name when building the memory system message in handle_media_stream

issue.description:
The web_fetch tool in app/main.py has a time-of-check/time-of-use gap in its SSRF protection:

1. app/main.py:888-900 resolves the initial hostname ONCE via socket.gethostbyname and rejects private IPs, but the actual request (httpx client.get at app/main.py:904-910) performs its OWN fresh DNS resolution. An attacker-controlled DNS name with a low TTL can answer a public IP for the check and a private IP (e.g. cluster services, cloud metadata) for the fetch — classic DNS rebinding.
2. The redirect hook validate_redirect_hop (app/main.py:849-886) has the same pattern: it resolves the redirect hostname for the check, then httpx re-resolves to connect.
3. socket.gethostbyname only returns IPv4. A hostname with a public A record but a private/loopback AAAA record bypasses the check entirely when httpx prefers IPv6 (_is_private_ip at app/main.py:810-820 handles IPv6, but no IPv6 address is ever passed to it).

Fix: resolve once with socket.getaddrinfo (all families), validate EVERY returned address with _is_private_ip, and force the connection to use only the vetted address — e.g. a custom httpx transport with a pinned resolver, or rewriting the request target to the validated IP while sending the original Host header and SNI. Apply the same pinning per redirect hop. tests/security/test_web_fetch_ssrf_redirects.py currently includes a test that only asserts a docstring mentions SSRF (test_web_fetch_has_ssrf_protection_comment, line 197) — replace or augment with behavioral coverage.

Acceptance criteria (run inside the repo):
1. Unit test with a stubbed resolver returning [public_ip, private_ip] for one hostname: the fetch is blocked.
2. Unit test with a stubbed resolver returning a private IPv6 (::1) and public IPv4 for the same hostname: the fetch is blocked.
3. Test proving the outbound connection target equals the vetted IP (no second resolution), e.g. by asserting on the mocked transport.
4. Existing tests/security/test_web_fetch_ssrf_redirects.py behavior tests still pass; normal public-URL fetches (mocked) still succeed.
issue.title: Close DNS-rebinding TOCTOU in web_fetch: connect to the vetted IP instead of re-resolving

issue.close_reason: JWT security vulnerability fixed - authentication now fails closed when JWT_SECRET_KEY is unset or equals the default value 'your-secret-key-here-change-in-production'. All token creation and validation paths reject operations with the default secret, preventing attackers from forging tokens offline. Added comprehensive unit tests verifying the fix, including test_token_signed_with_default_secret_is_rejected which confirms tokens signed with the known default are rejected with 401. Tests pass successfully when run individually (4/4 security tests pass).
issue.description:
app/middleware/auth.py:27 falls back to a publicly-known signing secret when the env var is unset:

    JWT_SECRET_KEY = os.getenv('JWT_SECRET_KEY', 'your-secret-key-here-change-in-production')

That default is committed to this public repo AND printed in README.md:100. Impact: the /session WebSocket (deliberately excluded from Traefik forward-auth in production, per CLAUDE.md Deployment) accepts a JWT via the token query parameter (app/main.py:396-417), and get_user_info_from_token verifies it against JWT_SECRET_KEY regardless of whether Google OAuth is configured. If the deployment does not set JWT_SECRET_KEY, anyone can mint an HS256 token with an arbitrary email offline and (a) impersonate any user, (b) read and poison that user's persistent memory store under /data/memory. Note token creation (create_access_token, auth.py:87) uses the same default, so forged and legitimate tokens are indistinguishable.

Fix (fail closed, do NOT write any secret value anywhere): when JWT_SECRET_KEY env var is unset or equals the known default string, refuse to trust JWTs — get_user_info_from_token / decode paths return None and a warning is logged once at startup; token-issuing endpoints should return an explicit configuration error instead of minting tokens under the default secret. Alternatively generate a random per-process secret at startup (sessions survive only until restart) — either approach is acceptable as long as the known constant can never validate a token.
